text: Welcome back to Front Desk, the podcast for people who run hotels. Today I want to tell you about the most useful complaint I ever received, because it changed how I train every person at my reception desk. A guest came down at eleven at night and told me the room was unacceptable. Her exact word. Unacceptable. Now, my first instinct was to defend the room, because I had checked that room myself that afternoon and there was nothing wrong with it. But I have learned something over fifteen years in this job: the first complaint is almost never the real one. It is just the one that is easiest to say out loud at eleven at night. So instead of explaining, I asked one question. I said, what happened tonight? And she told me. She had a video call with her team in Singapore at nine, and the internet dropped four times. She missed the call. By the time she came downstairs, the room had become the enemy, because the room was the only thing in the building she could point at. The internet was the problem. The room was just the messenger. Here is what I did, and here is why. I did not apologise for the room, because the room was fine and she knew it. An apology for the wrong thing tells the guest you were not listening. I apologised for the call she missed. Then I moved her to a room on the second floor, where the signal is strongest, and I gave her the direct number of our night technician so she would not have to come downstairs again. She wrote to me two months later to book the same week. So my advice to you is this. When a guest complains, do not solve the sentence they said. Find the sentence they did not say. Ask what happened, listen to the whole answer without preparing your defence while they speak, and only then decide what to offer. It takes ninety seconds longer, and it saves the guest.
